0: The question behind this project is whether a CNN improves clothing classification compared with two classical approaches using pixel values. This is a supervised multiclass classification task: each input is an image and each target is one of ten categories. A useful output is a correct category for an unseen benchmark image. I chose this comparison because it lets me investigate the value of a model designed for images while keeping the dataset and evaluation observations consistent. I also wanted to understand the errors, rather than stop at one overall score. This is a benchmark experiment; I have not built or tested a system for ordinary shopping photographs. I will explain the preparation and model choices, then use the final results and errors to answer the question.
1: Fashion-MNIST provides 28 by 28 grayscale images in ten labelled categories. There are 60,000 official development images and a separate 10,000-image test set. Every class has the same number of observations. The examples show that the task includes both footwear and visually similar upper-body garments. The small, standardised images keep the experiments manageable, but they also limit how much visual detail is available.
2:
I checked the development data for missing values, invalid labels, pixel ranges, constant images and exact duplicates. None of those checks required removing observations. I scaled pixels from zero to 255 into zero to one by dividing by 255. Logistic regression and kNN use a flattened vector of 784 pixel features; the CNN keeps the two-dimensional grid. From the official 60,000-image development pool I used 48,000 for training and 12,000 for validation, using the same observations for every model. The split was stratified and group-aware, so class proportions were preserved and any identical images would stay together. No exact duplicates were actually found. The official 10,000 test images were reserved for final scoring. This is one fixed hold-out split, not five-fold cross-validation, even though the splitting tool was StratifiedGroupKFold.

Automatic demonstration: the grid scan starts on entry, progresses through the 784 pixels in row order, and updates the pixel intensity, divided-by-255 value and marker in the flattened plot. No hovering is needed. It pauses off-screen or while notes are open. Reduced motion keeps it static, with optional pointer inspection.
3:
Say (60 seconds): Every class is exactly 10% of every subset: 4,800/48,000 training, 1,200/12,000 validation and 1,000/10,000 official test images. Equal proportions let us compare models without changing the class mix.

Implementation: notebook 01 uses StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42), then next(splitter.split(np.zeros(len(labels)), labels, groups)). This takes only the first yielded split: fold 0 is validation and folds 1–4 are training. We used one fixed 80/20 split, NOT five-fold cross-validation: there was no rotation through five model evaluations.

Defend the distinction: stratification preserves class proportions. Grouping uses hashes of original uint8 pixels to keep identical images together. No exact duplicate groups were found, so grouping was a precaution; we did not remove duplicates. All three models used the same saved source indices, confirmed by matching split fingerprints in their metadata.

The test set was provided by Fashion-MNIST; we checked its balance rather than constructing it. Exact balance was verified for this dataset, not assumed as a guarantee for arbitrary groups. A historical test-file integrity audit computed no model scores.

Sources: notebook 01; saved split metadata and NPZ; final class-counts.csv; model metadata.
4: I used logistic regression as a linear reference and kNN as a reference based on pixel similarity. They use the same flattened images, which makes the comparison straightforward. For logistic regression I compared C values of 0.01, 0.1, 1 and 10. C controls the inverse strength of L2 regularisation: a smaller C penalises large weights more strongly. C equals 0.1 had the highest validation accuracy, so it was selected. Its advantage over C equals 1 was only ten validation images, which is a modest preference. Increasing C to 10 improved training accuracy but reduced validation accuracy, consistent with weaker regularisation overfitting. For kNN I compared three, five and nine neighbours using Euclidean distance and equal voting. Three neighbours gave the highest validation accuracy. I did not exhaustively search every distance metric or preprocessing option. kNN and logistic regression were almost tied on validation accuracy, so I do not claim a decisive ranking between them from that split.

6: The CNN keeps the image grid and learns local patterns using two convolutional layers. The selected model has 32 filters in the first layer and 64 in the second, each using a three by three kernel and padding of one. Each convolution is followed by ReLU and two by two max pooling. The feature maps shrink from 28 by 28 to 14 by 14 and then seven by seven. I flatten those maps, use a 128-unit hidden layer with ReLU, apply dropout of 0.25, and produce ten output scores. ReLU supplies nonlinearity with a simple computation; I did not compare it against Leaky ReLU experimentally. Pooling reduces spatial resolution and computation. Dropout was included to reduce overfitting. The final layer returns raw logits. CrossEntropyLoss handles log-softmax internally during training, so I do not add a separate softmax before that loss. For reporting probabilities I apply softmax to the logits. The largest score or probability determines the predicted class.
7:
Say (60 seconds): Feature maps show internal activations; these maps ask how a selected output score depends on the input. Gradient saliency measures the absolute derivative of that class logit with respect to each normalised pixel. Occlusion covers a 5×5 grey patch and records how the same class logit changes. The map highlights positive mean score drops. The moving patch readout also preserves negative changes, where covering a region increases the score. These are two different diagnostics and can disagree. For Shirt #32, compare the predicted Coat score with the true Shirt score. Neither map proves why shirts are generally harder.

Demonstration: start on the existing validation Coat #22; show gradient saliency, select Occlusion map, then let the patch scan play automatically; no manual start is needed. It pauses automatically when leaving the slide or opening notes. If time allows, select Shirt, compare Coat (predicted) versus Shirt (true class) in the target selector. Allow no more than one minute for the main demonstration.

Implementation: the frozen selected wider CNN is in evaluation mode (dropout off). Input autograd is enabled for saliency; evaluation mode does not mean gradients are disabled. Use raw class logits, not softmax probabilities, so scores and differences are not percentages. Targets remain fixed during masking. Use original normalised pixels for all diagnostics. The patch fill is 0.5, size 5×5, stride 2, with final edge start 23 included, giving 169 positions. Original-minus-occluded logit is retained per patch; per-pixel occlusion averages signed changes from every patch covering that pixel. The heatmap clips negative means to zero, while the patch readout shows signed changes. All maps are independently scaled to their own maximum, so brightness cannot be compared across images or methods. The class selector offers the predicted class, plus the actual class when different.

Limits: gradient maps describe local sensitivity and can be noisy. Occlusion results depend on baseline and patch size, and masking can create unrealistic inputs. Neither is a causal explanation or segmentation mask. Do not infer what a specific channel recognises, or claim these examples explain population-level shirt difficulty. These are the ten existing deterministic validation examples, not chosen for attractive heatmaps. Computed offline with the original checkpoint hash, and base predictions checked against saved outputs; no retraining, test inference, model selection or change to final metrics. The browser displays recorded measurements rather than running a model. Reduced motion disables automatic scanning; slider and one-patch stepping remain available.

Sources: W10/10-CNNs-block2.pdf, pages 56–60; presentation/editorial/build_interpretation.py; interpretation.json; original frozen CNN checkpoint and saved validation examples.
8: I evaluated two architecture widths. The original network used 16 and 32 convolutional filters and a 64-unit hidden layer. The wider network doubled those widths to 32, 64 and 128. There were four initial runs: the original baseline, an extended run of that architecture, the wider model, and the wider model with weight decay. The baseline reached 90.70 percent validation accuracy; the extended run reached 91.45; the wider model reached 92.33. I trained from scratch with Adam and a learning rate of 0.001. Within a run I restored the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss, and between configurations I used validation accuracy as the main selection metric. I then added four runs to compare the two wider configurations across three seeds each: eight CNN training runs in total. Their mean accuracy difference was only 0.061 percentage points. Weight decay gave lower observed variation and better average shirt recall. I retained the previously selected original seed-42 wider checkpoint rather than choosing the best seed afterward.
9: These curves explain why the final epoch is not automatically the best model. The selected CNN checkpoint is epoch 12, where validation loss reached its minimum of about 0.222. Training loss continued to decline after that while validation loss remained higher, which is evidence of overfitting with further training. Validation accuracy did improve slightly later, but our within-run selection rule was lowest validation loss, which also reflects confidence in the predictions. At the selected checkpoint training accuracy was 95.67 percent and validation accuracy was 92.33 percent, a gap of 3.33 percentage points. Early stopping ended the run at epoch 17 and restored epoch 12. Logistic regression had a smaller selected gap of 2.02 points. Its limited gains from weaker regularisation suggest limited representational capacity, but do not prove pure underfitting. For kNN ordinary training accuracy would include each image as its own neighbour, so I did not use that as evidence of generalisation.
10: Before opening the test set for final scoring, I checked that the three model files matched the frozen fingerprints and reproduced all saved validation predictions on CPU with zero disagreements. I then evaluated those existing models without refitting. Logistic regression achieved 84.33 percent test accuracy, kNN 85.04, and the CNN 91.79. The CNN correctly classified 9,179 of the 10,000 images. Its test advantage was 6.75 percentage points over kNN and 7.46 over logistic regression. Its validation-to-test difference was about 0.54 points. The CNN had been selected as the primary model using validation evidence before these test results. Test scores were not used to change hyperparameters, epochs or seeds. Macro-F1 gives the same broad picture and per-class results explain what the overall scores hide.
11: Here I report recall for each actual category: of all the items that really belong to a class, how many did the model identify correctly? This is the useful meaning of accuracy within a true class. I avoid calling one-versus-rest accuracy a per-class score because the many negatives could make it misleading. Each test category has 1,000 images. The CNN identifies 99 percent of bags and 98.6 percent of trousers, but only 67.6 percent of shirts. It correctly identifies 676 shirts and misses 324. It improves shirt recall compared with both baselines, but that remains a major weakness. The CNN also does not win every individual category: kNN has slightly higher ankle-boot recall, 97.3 percent versus 97.0 percent. That is only three test images and should not be overstated.
12:
Say (75 seconds): Shirt recall is 676/1,000 = 67.6%; 324 actual shirts were missed. Shirt → T-shirt/top is 127 versus 63 in reverse; Shirt → Coat is 89 versus 32; Shirt → Pullover is 71 versus 32. Confusion runs both ways, but more often from shirts into these categories.

Observed: classes are balanced, shirt recall is lower, and these counts come from the CNN test confusion matrix. Rows are actual classes; columns are predictions. Both directions have 1,000 actual source-class images. Equal class sizes do not imply equal difficulty or symmetric errors.

Interpretation: overlapping silhouettes, limited detail at 28×28 pixels, and potentially more variation within shirts are plausible explanations. We have not proven those causes or measured greater within-class variation. Pictures do not prove causation or wrong labels.

Examples: each picture is the first saved test index matching that error direction. These are genuine illustrative cases, not a random or representative sample. Click to inspect the true label, saved prediction and ID. The optional gallery retains the original random sample.

Defend the totals: these three outgoing pairs cover 287 of 324 missed shirts; 37 went to other classes. No training, new inference or tuning was performed.

13: The results apply to this benchmark, with balanced classes and equal error costs. They do not establish performance on phone photographs, different backgrounds or lighting. Repeated decisions on one validation set can overfit development choices, and three training seeds do not measure uncertainty across different data splits. The models differ in capacity and training as well as how they use spatial structure, so this is not a controlled causal isolation of convolution. The final audit found no exact images shared between the development pool and the test set, although that does not exclude near duplicates. I retained the checkpoints trained on 48,000 images so the final evaluation corresponds exactly to the reviewed models; I did not refit on all 60,000.
14: The CNN is the strongest overall model among the approaches tested: 91.79 percent test accuracy, compared with about 84 to 85 percent for the classical baselines. This supports using a model designed for image patterns on this task, while not isolating the effect of spatial structure alone. The improvement does not remove the main weakness: shirts are still frequently confused with other upper-body garments. If very fast CPU prediction and a simple linear model are the priority, logistic regression remains a useful baseline; the existing matched validation timing shows it is much faster, although that timing is specific to our hardware and excludes loading and preprocessing. The main lesson is that data preparation, validation and error analysis are needed to make the headline accuracy meaningful. A future experiment could investigate augmentation or different image representations using fresh development evidence; I would not tune those changes on this test set.
